analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder for OSHA to cite employers for workplace safety violations.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before the 106th Congress ended, so OSHA's citation rules were unchanged.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules OSHA uses to cite employers for safety violations. OSHA could no longer cite an employer unless the employer knew — or with reasonable diligence should have known — about the violation. Employers could also escape a citation by showing they had trained workers and set work rules, blaming the violation on employees who broke those rules, and could get citations thrown out by showing they used alternative methods that were just as protective as the official standard.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing OSHA citations. The bill gave them a knowledge requirement, an 'employee misbehavior' defense, and an alternative-methods defense, all of which would make citations harder to issue and easier to overturn.

how_it_helps.text: Bars OSHA from citing an employer unless the employer knew, or with reasonable diligence would have known, of the alleged violation.
Lets an employer avoid a citation by showing it provided training and equipment, communicated work rules, and that employees' failure to follow those rules caused the violation.
Requires that a citation be vacated if the employer shows workers were protected by alternative methods at least as protective as the violated standard.

analysis.who_pays: Workers. Weakened citations mean less deterrence of unsafe conditions and fewer corrections, so the risk of on-the-job injury and death would shift back onto employees, whose safety complaints and injuries would be easier for employers to attribute to 'employee error.'

drawbacks.text: The 'employee failure to observe work rules' defense lets an employer defeat a citation by pointing to training paperwork, even where the hazard itself persisted and a worker was hurt — moving accountability for workplace safety from the employer to the worker.

A good-faith argument for the bill is that the existing standard lets OSHA cite employers who had no way of knowing about a violation, which employers view as strict liability; the bill would align penalties with employer knowledge and reward documented safety programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Employers would gain real protection from citations they could not have prevented, but the bulk of the benefit is a lower risk of citation overall, because almost any employer with written rules and training records could shift blame to the worker. The cost falls on worker safety enforcement: fewer citations mean less pressure to fix dangerous conditions before someone gets hurt.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee and its Workforce Protections Subcommittee and died there when the 106th Congress ended, without ever getting a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ralph Hall (D-TX) introduced the bill on July 27, 2000, joined by Rep. Billy Tauzin (R-LA); it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On September 20, 2000, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, the last recorded action.
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers. Because the bill never became law, the existing OSHA citation standard stayed in place and employers did not gain the new defenses against citations. Employers seeking reduced liability gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Ralph M. Hall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would make OSHA citations harder to issue and easier to overturn.

for.name: Rep. W.J. 'Billy' Tauzin
for.what_they_did: Joined Hall in introducing the bill at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action beyond sending it to a subcommittee; it never came to a markup or vote.

against.name: Rep. William F. Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never scheduled the bill for consideration before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced the bill and its only recorded cosponsors were two Republicans, but the Republican-led committee never acted on it, so no vote ever tested the split.

industries.note: The bill would have made citations harder to issue and easier to defeat, cutting employer liability for workplace violations. The trade-off is weaker deterrence of unsafe conditions, whose cost falls on workers in the form of injury risk.

OSHA would have lost its ability to hold employers responsible for violations they could have discovered, narrowing its core enforcement tool. Its interest in enforcement runs alongside workers' interest in safe conditions.
